turns.text: Can you describe your first morning waking up in Beidahuang after leaving Shanghai? What did you see, hear, and feel?

The first morning, I woke up before the sun rose, because the cold had crept into my bones and I couldn’t sleep through it. The air in the dormitory was thick with the smell of damp straw and unwashed clothes, and I could hear the heavy breathing of the other girls, some snoring, some whispering quietly to themselves. I pulled on my coat before even sitting up, because the wind found every crack in the walls. When I stepped outside, the sky was a deep, bruised blue, and the fields stretched out flat and endless, nothing like the crowded lanes of home. I heard the creak of the pump handle at the well, the distant clatter of someone’s bucket, and the low voices of the older workers already moving toward the fields. My breath came out in white clouds. I felt smaller than I ever had in Shanghai, as if I’d been dropped into a place where nobody knew me and nothing I’d learned before mattered. The ground was muddy and uneven, so every step was careful, and I remember thinking: this is not a place you visit, it’s a place you survive.

It’s striking how the cold and the unfamiliar sounds made everything feel so foreign, and I can almost picture the endless fields you describe. When you first saw those other girls in the dormitory, whispering or snoring, did you feel any sense of connection with them, or was it more like you were all alone together?

At first, it was definitely more like being alone together. We all came from different corners of the city, but in that room, our shyness and fear made us strangers. I remember lying on my narrow bunk, listening to the whispers in the dark, and feeling like I was eavesdropping on secrets I wasn’t part of. In the mornings, we avoided each other’s eyes, busying ourselves with folding quilts or lacing up shoes, as if any glance might betray how lost we felt. There was a heaviness between us, like nobody wanted to be the first to admit how much we missed home. The only time we really connected was when someone cried at night—then, for a moment, the silence would break, and someone might whisper a few comforting words, but the next day it was back to pretending we were brave.

I remember one night when the wind was especially loud, rattling the window so hard I thought the glass would break. Someone started sobbing quietly, trying to muffle it with her sleeve. I lay there listening, heart pounding, because her crying sounded just like how I felt inside. I wanted to reach out, but I was afraid of making her shame worse, or maybe of exposing my own weakness. Instead, I pulled my blanket tighter and stared at the ceiling, counting the cracks. The next morning, she acted as if nothing had happened, and so did everyone else. We were all trying to hold ourselves together, each of us afraid that if we let go, we’d never stop falling apart. That feeling of being surrounded by people but still completely alone—that’s what I remember most from those early days.

The way you describe lying awake, listening but unable to reach out, really shows how isolation can feel even in a crowded room. When you counted the cracks in the ceiling that night, did you find yourself thinking about home, or did your mind go somewhere else to cope?

Mostly, I thought about home, but not in a way that brought comfort. I pictured my mother’s kitchen, the chipped blue bowl she used for rice, the way sunlight fell through the window onto the table. I tried to imagine what she might be doing at that exact moment—maybe boiling water, maybe folding laundry. Sometimes those thoughts made the ache sharper, so I’d force myself to focus on the cracks above me instead, tracing their shapes and making up stories about them: one looked like a river, another like a tree. It was a way to keep my mind busy, to push back the homesickness for a little while. But the smell of the straw mattress, the sound of the wind, always pulled me back to where I was.

Sometimes I’d count the cracks over and over, as if there was some secret number that would unlock a way out. Other times, I’d listen to the wind and try to convince myself it sounded like the traffic from Shanghai, just far away. But the truth was, no matter what I did, the room always felt foreign, and my body never forgot that I didn’t belong. There were moments when I tried to remember the slogans we’d been taught, thinking maybe if I believed in them hard enough, the emptiness would fade. But those words felt thin compared to the weight of missing home. The cracks and the wind became my company at night—familiar, but never comforting.

Your memories of the wind and the cracks almost seem like a language of survival, something private that helped you get through the nights. You mentioned trying to believe in the slogans you’d learned—was there ever a moment, maybe during work or meetings, when you felt pressure to act more enthusiastic or loyal than you really felt inside?

All the time. During meetings, we’d stand in rows and recite slogans in unison, our voices echoing off the bare walls. I remember the way my cheeks would ache from forcing a smile, and how I’d clap along with everyone else, trying to match the rhythm so nobody would notice if my heart wasn’t in it. Sometimes, when the leaders asked questions, I’d raise my hand and say what I thought they wanted to hear, even if it didn’t feel true. There was a constant worry that if you showed any hesitation, someone might report you, or at least look at you differently. The pressure was a kind of performance—we were all actors, pretending to be more certain and devoted than we really were, because to do otherwise felt dangerous. At night, the gap between what I said in public and what I felt in private was so wide it made me dizzy.

There were days when I felt like I was watching myself from the outside, mouthing the right words while my mind drifted somewhere far away. I remember one meeting after a particularly hard week in the fields, when my hands were cracked and bleeding from the cold. They asked for volunteers to share “inspirational stories,” and I forced myself to stand up, repeating something about the “glory of labor.” My voice sounded empty to my own ears, but I saw relief in the faces around me—nobody wanted to be singled out, so we protected each other by playing our parts. The real loyalty was to survival, not to the slogans. Later, when I washed my hands in freezing water, I wondered if anyone believed any of it, or if we were all just waiting for someone else to drop the mask first.

The detail about your cracked hands and the “glory of labor” story really shows how much your body and spirit were at odds with the words you had to say. When you washed your hands that night, did you ever talk with anyone else about how you really felt, or was it something you always kept to yourself?

Mostly, I kept it to myself. The fear of saying the wrong thing was too strong, and trust was fragile—one careless word could change everything. Sometimes, while washing up, someone might mutter a complaint about the cold or the blisters, but it was always vague, never touching the deeper doubts we all carried. There was one girl who would sometimes look at me and raise her eyebrows, as if to say, “This is all nonsense, isn’t it?” But even then, we never said it out loud. The risk felt too great. So I learned to swallow my real feelings, to nod and agree, and to let the steam from the washbasin hide my face for a moment. The loneliness of not being able to speak honestly was almost as heavy as the work itself.

I remember the sting of the water on my cracked skin, and the way the steam rose in little clouds, almost like a shield. Sometimes I’d catch someone’s eye and see the same exhaustion, the same wariness, but we’d both look away quickly. The walls felt thin, and you never knew who might be listening just beyond them. Even when we were alone, the habit of caution lingered. I learned to talk about the weather, or how heavy the buckets were, but never about the ache in my chest or the emptiness behind my words. There were moments when I wanted to shout the truth just to hear it spoken, but I always bit it back. The silence was a kind of armor—uncomfortable, but necessary.

Your description of the silence as armor really stays with me—it makes me wonder how you found ways to keep going, day after day, when you couldn’t share what was really on your mind. Was there anything—an object, a routine, or even a small act—that helped you hold onto yourself during that time?
